content: 1. Douglas NM, Lampah DA, Kenangalem E, Simpson JA, Poespoprodjo JR, Sugiarto P, et al. conducted a hospital-based surveillance study in Southern Papua, which revealed that severe anemia caused by non-falciparum malaria species represents a significant health burden in the region. This study was published in PLoS Medicine in 2013 (10(12): e1001575). 2. Poespoprodjo JR, Fobia W, Kenangalem E, Lampah DA, Hasanuddin A, Warikar N, et al. identified vivax malaria as a major cause of morbidity in early infancy. Their findings were published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2009 (48(12): 1704-1712). 3. Genton B, D'Acremont V, Rare L, Baea K, Reeder JC, Alpers MP, et al. demonstrated that Plasmodium vivax and mixed infections are associated with severe malaria in children. This prospective cohort study was conducted in Papua New Guinea and published in PLoS Medicine in 2008 (5(6): e127). 4. Kochar DK, Das A, Kochar SK, Saxena V, Sirohi P, Garg S, et al. reported on a series of severe Plasmodium vivax malaria cases from Bikaner in northwestern India. Their findings were published in the American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene in 2009 (80(2): 194-198). 5. Alexandre MA, Ferreira CO, Siqueira AM, Magalhães BL, Mourão MPG, Lacerda MV, et al. documented severe Plasmodium vivax malaria cases in the Brazilian Amazon. This study was published in Emerging Infectious Diseases in 2010 (16(10): 1611-1614). 6. Nosten F, McGready R, Simpson JA, Thwai KL, Balkan S, Cho T, et al. investigated the effects of Plasmodium vivax malaria during pregnancy. Their findings were published in The Lancet in 1999 (354(9178): 546-549). 7. William T, Menon J, Rajahram G, Chan L, Ma G, Donaldson S, et al. described severe Plasmodium knowlesi malaria cases in a tertiary care hospital in Sabah, Malaysia. This study was published in Emerging Infectious Diseases in 2011 (17(7): 1248-1255). 8. Barber BE, William T, Grigg MJ, Menon J, Auburn S, Marfurt J, et al. conducted a prospective comparative study in Sabah, Malaysia, comparing knowlesi, falciparum, and vivax malaria. They found a high proportion of severe disease in Plasmodium knowlesi and vivax cases but no mortality with early referral and artesunate therapy. This study was published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2013 (56(3): 383-397). 9. Grigg MJ, William T, Barber BE, Parameswaran U, Bird E, Piera K, et al. evaluated the combination of parasite lactate dehydrogenase-based and histidine-rich protein 2-based rapid diagnostic tests to improve specificity for diagnosing malaria caused by Plasmodium knowlesi and other species in Sabah, Malaysia. Their findings were published in the Journal of Clinical Microbiology in 2014 (52(6): 2053-2060). 10. Gogtay N, Kannan S, Thatte UM, Olliaro PL, Sinclair D reviewed the efficacy of artemisinin-based combination therapy for treating uncomplicated Plasmodium vivax malaria. This systematic review was published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews in 2013 (10): CD008492. 11. The World Health Organization (WHO) released a policy brief in 2016 emphasizing the importance of testing for G6PD deficiency to ensure the safe use of primaquine in the radical cure of Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium ovale infections. 12. WHO published a guide in 2018 on G6PD deficiency rapid diagnostic testing to support the radical cure of Plasmodium vivax malaria. 13. Milligan R, Daher A, Villanueva G, Bergman H, Graves P reviewed alternative dosing schedules of primaquine for preventing malaria relapse in individuals with Plasmodium vivax. This review was published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews in 2020. 14. Commons RJ, Simpson JA, Thriemer K, Chu CS, Douglas NM, Abreha T, et al. conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on the hematological consequences of Plasmodium vivax malaria after chloroquine treatment, with and without primaquine. Their findings were published in BMC Medicine in 2019 (17(1): 151). 15. Galappaththy GNL, Tharyan P, Kirubakaran R reviewed the use of primaquine for preventing relapse in individuals with Plasmodium vivax malaria treated with chloroquine. This review was published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews in 2013 (10): CD004389. 16. Radeva-Petrova D, Kayentao K, ter Kuile FO, Sinclair D, Garner P reviewed the efficacy of drugs for preventing malaria in pregnant women in endemic areas. This systematic review was published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews in 2014 (10): CD000169. 17. WHO published the third edition of the Management of Severe Malaria: A Practical Handbook in 2013, providing comprehensive guidance on managing severe malaria cases. 18. Sinclair D, Donegan S, Isba R, Lalloo DG reviewed the comparative efficacy of artesunate versus quinine for treating severe malaria. This review was published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews in 2012 (6): CD005967. 19. WHO released an information note in 2013 on delayed hemolytic anemia following treatment with artesunate, highlighting the need for monitoring and management. 20. Hendriksen ICE, Mtove G, Kent A, Gesase S, Reyburn H, Lemnge MM, et al. studied the population pharmacokinetics of intramuscular artesunate in African children with severe malaria, providing insights into practical dosing regimens. This study was published in Clinical Pharmacology and Therapeutics in 2013 (93(5): 443-450). 21. Zaloumis SG, Tarning J, Krishna S, Price RN, White NJ, Davis TME, et al. conducted a pooled analysis of the population pharmacokinetics of intravenous artesunate in patients with severe malaria. Their findings were published in CPT: Pharmacometrics & Systems Pharmacology in 2014 (3: e145). 22. Esu E, Effa EE, Opie ON, Uwaoma A, Meremikwu MM reviewed the use of artemether for severe malaria. This review was published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews in 2014 (9): CD010678. 23. Okebe J, Eisenhut M reviewed the use of pre-referral rectal artesunate for severe malaria. This review was published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews in 2014 (5): CD009964. 24. WHO updated its guidelines in 2023 on the use of rectal artesunate as a pre-referral treatment for severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria. 25. WHO's prequalification program, managed by the United Nations, ensures the quality and safety of antimalarial drugs. This program was established in 2009. 26. WHO published methods for monitoring antimalarial drug efficacy in 2009, providing a framework for surveillance and evaluation. 27. WHO released a report in 2020 summarizing 10 years of surveillance on antimalarial drug efficacy, resistance, and response (2010–2019). 28. Ajayi IO, Browne EN, Bateganya F, Yar D, Happi C, Falade CO, et al. evaluated the effectiveness of artemisinin-based combination therapy in the context of home management of malaria in sub-Saharan Africa. Their findings were published in Malaria Journal in 2008 (7: 190). 29. WHO published a practical handbook in 2008 on the pharmacovigilance of antimalarial medicines, emphasizing safety monitoring. 30. Stresman G, Whittaker C, Slater HC, Bousema T, Cook J quantified the clustering of Plasmodium falciparum infections within households to inform malaria control strategies. This study was published in PLoS Medicine in 2020 (17(10): e1003370). 31. Sandfort M, Vantaux A, Kim S, Obadia T, Pepey A, Gardais S, et al. investigated the occupational and spatial clustering of malaria risk in Cambodia, focusing on forest malaria. Their findings were published in Malaria Journal in 2020 (19(1): 413). 32. Smith C, Whittaker M cautioned against the use of stigmatizing terminology in malaria elimination settings. Their commentary was published in Malaria Journal in 2014 (13: 377). 33. WHO published the third edition of the International Health Regulations in 2016, providing a framework for global health security. 34. WHO released a guide in 2006 on monitoring and evaluating communicable disease surveillance and response systems. 35. WHO published a technical brief in 2020 to assist countries in preparing malaria funding requests for the Global Fund (2020–2022). 36. Alonso-Coello P, Schünemann HJ, Moberg J, Brignardello-Petersen R, Akl EA, Davoli M, et al. introduced the GRADE Evidence to Decision (EtD) frameworks, a systematic approach to making informed healthcare decisions. This was published in 2013. 37. The GRADE Working Group published the GRADE Handbook in 2013, providing an introduction to the methodology for grading recommendations, assessment, development, and evaluation. 38. Schandelmaier S, Briel M, Varadhan R, Schmid CH, Devasenapathy N, Hayward RA, et al. developed the ICEMAN instrument to assess the credibility of effect modification analyses in randomized controlled trials and meta-analyses. This study was published in CMAJ in 2020 (192(32): E901-E906). 39. Santesso N, Glenton C, Dahm P, Garner P, Akl EA, Alper B, et al. provided GRADE guidelines for creating informative statements to communicate findings from systematic reviews of interventions. This was published in the Journal of Clinical Epidemiology in 2020 (119: 126-135). 40. WHO summarized the conclusions and recommendations from the October 2021 meeting of the Strategic Advisory Group of Experts on Immunization in the Weekly Epidemiological Record (96(50): 613-632). 41. WHO documented the 20th meeting of the Malaria Policy Advisory Group in 2021, providing updates on malaria policy and strategy. 42. WHO updated its malaria terminology in 2021 to ensure clarity and consistency in communication.
